# ThreadPoolPro v1.0.0

The first stable release of **ThreadPoolPro**, a high-performance work-stealing C++ thread pool for modern C++.

## Highlights

- Lock-free, per-worker Chase-Lev work-stealing deques for local task storage.
- Type-erased task storage with small-buffer optimization — no allocation for small, nothrow-movable callables.
- Sharded, mutex-guarded injection queues for submissions from non-worker threads.
- Lightweight `Future`/`ResultState` replacing `std::packaged_task` + `std::future`.
- Process-wide `ThreadMarket` of leased, persistent OS threads — cheap pool construction/destruction after warm-up.
- Atomic wake-token park/wait for worker synchronization instead of `condition_variable` + mutex.
- `enqueue()` (with result) and `detach()` (fire-and-forget) submission APIs.
- Pause/resume support for in-flight task execution.
- Graceful and immediate shutdown modes (`FinishTasks` / `DiscardTasks`).
- `waitIdle()` — blocks until the pool drains, helping steal/execute tasks itself rather than sitting idle.
- Runtime statistics: active tasks, queued tasks, exception count, idle thread count.
- Move-only, exception-safe `Task` wrapper with explicit heap/inline storage paths.

## Performance

The implementation is designed to minimize contention and avoid unnecessary allocation on the hot submit/execute path.

- Local push/pop costs no atomic read-modify-write in the uncontended case.
- Randomized steal-victim offsets spread contention across workers instead of serializing on the same low-index victim.
- Sharded injection queues avoid a single shared lock becoming the dominant contention point as worker count grows.
- Small-buffer-optimized `Task` storage avoids a heap allocation per submitted callable in the common case.
- `ResultState` is a single, purpose-sized heap allocation per `enqueue()`, replacing `std::packaged_task`'s larger general-purpose shared state.
- Spin → yield → park backoff avoids paying park/wake syscall latency for short-lived bursts of work.
- `ThreadMarket` reuses already-running OS threads across `ThreadPool` lifetimes, avoiding thread-creation cost on repeated construction/destruction.

## Benchmarks

Measured against oneTBB at 10K / 100K / 1M iterations (and 1k–100k for
worker-count scaling). Full results: `benchmarks/results/v1_0_0.md`.

| Operation                          | ThreadPoolPro (1M) | oneTBB (1M) | Δ       |
|-------------------------------------|---------------------|-------------|---------|
| Detach (caught exception)          | 114.18 ms           | 133.30 ms   | +16.7%  |
| Detach Single Task                 | 376.76 ms           | 157.34 ms   | -58.2%  |
| Enqueue + Result                   | 941.76 ms           | 168.78 ms   | -82.1%  |
| Detach Batch + Drain (64 tasks)    | 50.60 s              | 3.44 s      | -93.2%  |
| Construct + Destroy                | 10.63 s              | 621.59 ms   | -94.2%  |
| Worker Count 32 (100k tasks)       | 26.38 s              | 1.30 s      | -95.1%  |
| Worker Count 8 (100k tasks)        | 92.94 s              | 1.29 s      | -98.6%  |

ThreadPoolPro currently trails oneTBB — a mature, heavily-tuned
production library — on nearly every apples-to-apples throughput
comparison, sometimes substantially so at higher worker counts and
batch sizes. The one exception measured is the caught-exception path
under `detach()`, where ThreadPoolPro is modestly faster.

Everything else measured (single-callable invoke, state queries, raw
queue push/pop/steal, move construction, pause/resume cycling) has no
oneTBB equivalent benchmarked here, so those numbers are reported
without a comparison baseline; see the full results file for the raw
figures.

This is a first release: the design choices documented throughout the
codebase (sharded injection queues, randomized steal offsets, the
SBO'd `Task`, the leased-thread `ThreadMarket`) address specific
contention points found during development, but oneTBB's task-stealing
scheduler has years of production tuning behind it that this library
doesn't yet match. Closing this gap is expected follow-up work rather
than a claim this release makes.

## Testing

The project includes a comprehensive test suite covering:

- Unit tests
- Integration tests
- Lifecycle tests
- Move semantics
- Regression tests
- Exception safety
- Task submission and retrieval (local queue, stealing, injection shards)
- Pause/resume behavior
- Shutdown modes (`FinishTasks` / `DiscardTasks`), including self-detach from within a running task
- Future/ResultState lifecycle, including error paths
- VTable operation round-trips (invoke, move, destroy, heap-delete)

## Code Coverage

The current test suite achieves:

- **93.3% line coverage** (513 / 550 lines)
- **96.9% function coverage** (377 / 389 functions)

Per-directory breakdown:

| Directory                          | Line Coverage | Function Coverage |
|-------------------------------------|---------------|--------------------|
| `include/ThreadPoolPro`             | 87.9% (29/33) | 97.7% (42/43)      |
| `include/ThreadPoolPro/Detail`      | 91.9% (102/111) | 96.6% (284/294)  |
| `src/ThreadPoolPro`                 | 94.3% (200/212) | 96.0% (24/25)    |
| `src/ThreadPoolPro/Detail`          | 93.8% (182/194) | 100.0% (27/27)   |

Coverage reports exclude test infrastructure and third-party dependencies, focusing on the `ThreadPoolPro` library implementation.

## Continuous Integration

Automated builds and tests are configured for:

- GCC — Debug
- GCC — Release
- Clang — Debug
- Clang — Release
- MSVC — Debug
- MSVC — Release
- AppleClang — Debug
- AppleClang — Release

## Release

This release represents the first stable version of ThreadPoolPro and establishes the initial API, synchronization design, testing infrastructure, and cross-platform CI pipeline.

## Installation

Clone the repository and integrate ThreadPoolPro into your C++ project using the provided CMake configuration, or install via the Conan recipe or vcpkg port under `packaging/`.

See the project documentation for build instructions, API usage, and integration details.
